newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy and Spain produce tough EMU budgets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy and Spain produce tough EMU budgets.

text.p: Italy and Spain produced tough austerity budgets on Friday in a last minute rush to get their economies into shape ahead planned economic and monetary union (EMU) in Europe.

Analysts said both countries might have done just enough to assure them of a place among founder members of the single European currency, but warned that the potent budget medicine could cause unpleasant side effects.

Even citizens of the wealthy northern country of Belgium, which is almost guaranteed a place in EMU, face belt tightening after their government announced a fresh hike in indirect taxes on Friday as it fine tunes its economy for Europe.

Debt-ladden Italy, which analysts say faces the most daunting task of the three states, was on Friday putting the finishing touches to a budget that aims to slash a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's public deficit.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said his centre-left government would introduce a one-off "Euro-tax" to raise 12.5 trillion lire, along with sweeping cuts to public spending.
The Spanish government, headed by rightist leader Jose Maria Aznar, announced more modest measures which will cut 1.2 trillion pesetas ($9.41 billion) off the 1997 deficit.

Both countries have to halve current levels of over-spending next year if they are to reduce their ratio of deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to the elusive three percent level demanded by the Maastricht Treaty.

Analysts doubted whether either Prodi or Aznar could meet the target, but said they might get close enough to persuade their northern European partners to let them climb onto the EMU boat from its launch in 1999.
"I don't think they'll cut the deficit-to-GDP target to three percent without resorting to accountancy tricks," said Dominic Konstam, economist with Credit Suisse First Boston.
"However there's a very good chance they'll both be in EMU from the start," he added, speaking from his office in London.

Belgium, which has already contained its annual deficit but suffers the highest debt to GDP ratio in the EU, also presented an exacting budget on Friday worth 80 billion francs ($2.55 billion), including the increase in indirect taxes.
Italy had originally planned to introduce a 32.4 trillion lire budget, but had to dramatically revise its package after a meeting between Prodi and Aznar earlier this month in Spain.
The Italian government had been looking to Spain to support its tentative bid to persuade European partners to relax stringent criteria for countries wishing to be part of EMU.
But Aznar, confident in the knowledge that Spain has a much smaller debt mountain and is enjoying stronger economic growth than Italy, refused.
Faced by the threat of being cast adrift with Greece on the southern rim of the Europe Union, Italy dramatically upped its budgetary rigour.

While analysts welcomed the move, they said there was a danger that the new fiscal tightening might push the wobbling Italian economy into recession. Spain's economy could also be stung by Aznar's harsh recipe for EMU.
They added that if Spain and Italy were now barred from EMU by their northern European partners, there would be a blood- bath on financial markets.
"If they are now excluded there would be a huge devaluation. The markets are gambling that Spain and Italy will make it," said Sally Wilkinson, an economist at Swiss bank UBS in London.
